paragraphs: A seedling grows new leaves. Later, a mature plant may flower and produce seeds. Growth brings changes in what a living thing can do.
Animals also grow before becoming capable of reproduction. Some hatch from eggs; others, including humans, are born as live young. Growing larger is only part of this journey.
Human development includes changes in the body, feelings and relationships. In this chapter, explore adolescence with curiosity, reliable information and respect for everyone’s privacy.

lesson.text: 6.1  Growing With Age

Human life includes infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age. **Adolescence**, usually ages 10–19, connects childhood and adulthood. People reach developmental milestones at different times.
Visiting his grandparents, Venkatesh notices that his 12-year-old cousin Devyani has grown taller. She notices his changed voice and thin moustache. What other changes occur while young people grow?

paragraphs: 1. On a slip, suggest a change between Grades 5 and 8: height, strength, appearance, interests or behaviour. Fictional examples are welcome.
2. Do not identify anyone or describe private experiences. Fold the slips into a jar. The teacher mixes and reads suitable slips.
3. Discuss respectfully, without guessing the writers. Group the ideas in your notebook using Table 6.1. Note a repeated idea and an unanswered question.
lesson.figureCaption: Anonymous slips can help a class discuss general changes without identifying anyone.

lesson.caption: Table 6.1  Organising the class discussion
rows: What to record in your notebook
A general change mentioned on the slips
An idea about growth or physical ability
An idea about skin, hair or voice
Ideas about feelings, interests or behaviour
lesson.note: Read across to sort the anonymous ideas. These are recording categories, not results or a checklist for judging classmates.

lesson.text: Repeated suggestions tell you about the ideas on the slips, not how often a change occurs in all adolescents. A classroom discussion cannot establish a timetable that every body must follow.
lesson.addition: Distinguish anonymous discussion evidence from a population survey.

lesson.text: Changes in the Body

items: **Height:** a period of faster growth, called a growth spurt, often occurs during adolescence. Its timing and length differ.

**Body structure:** height, weight and muscle strength change. Broader shoulders and a wider chest often develop in boys; breast development occurs in girls during typical puberty. Both experience changes in body shape.
**Body hair:** hair develops in the armpits and pubic region in both boys and girls. Facial hair, and sometimes chest or back hair, often becomes more noticeable in boys. The amount and timing vary.

lesson.text: These are general patterns, not rules for judging classmates. Growing later does not make someone less capable. Avoid jokes about height, weight, skin, voice or hair. Discuss an individual health concern privately with a health professional.
Why a Voice May Change

The **voice box**, or larynx, is a structure in the throat that contains the vocal folds. Air passing through vibrating vocal folds produces sound. During puberty, the larynx and vocal folds grow. The voice often becomes deeper, particularly in boys, and may temporarily crack as it changes.

The projection at the front of the larynx is commonly called the Adam’s apple. It may become more noticeable, but it is not prominent in everyone. Girls’ voice boxes grow too, usually with less marked changes in pitch. A visible neck swelling should not be identified from appearance alone.

lesson.caption: A simplified front view: the larynx and thyroid gland are different structures. Their relative positions are shown, not a diagnosis.

lesson.text: Understanding Pimples

**Acne** is a skin condition that may cause pimples. Hormonal changes can increase the oil made by skin glands. Oil and dead skin cells may block hair follicles; inflammation and bacteria can contribute. Acne is common during adolescence. It does not mean that a person is dirty, and it is not a reason for teasing.

Wash the face gently with a mild cleanser and water; avoid harsh scrubbing or squeezing pimples. Excessive washing can irritate skin. Ask a trusted adult to help seek professional advice if acne is painful, persistent, leaving scars or causing distress. Do not borrow someone else’s medicine or apply unknown mixtures.
Puberty Is Part of Adolescence

**Puberty** is the process of physical changes through which the body becomes capable of reproduction. It includes internal changes as well as visible ones. Adolescence is broader: it also includes emotional and social development. Reproductive maturity does not mean that a young person is ready for marriage or parenthood.
lesson.addition: Distinguish biological capability from adult readiness, connecting the source child-marriage project.

lesson.text: **Secondary sexual characteristics** are body features that develop at puberty but are not the reproductive organs themselves. Examples include breast development and changes in facial hair and voice. These traits vary and should not be used to label or judge individuals.

paragraphs: Two learners of the same age differ in height and voice. Does being taller mean being more mature in every way? What evidence is missing?
Explain why appearance alone cannot establish health, emotional readiness or abilities. Suggest a respectful response.
lesson.addition: Reason about limits of visible evidence and the distinction between kinds of maturity.

lesson.text: 6.2  Reproductive Development

During puberty, reproductive organs mature gradually. These internal changes cannot all be seen from outside. In girls, the beginning of the **menstrual cycle** is one sign of this development. The cycle is a recurring sequence of changes involving the ovaries and the uterus.

The uterus develops an inner lining. When pregnancy does not occur, some of this lining leaves the body with blood through the vagina. This is **menstruation**, also called a period. Menstrual blood is not dirty or poisonous. Menstruation is a normal body process, not an illness.

lesson.caption: Count a menstrual cycle from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. The interval is not identical for everyone.

lesson.text: A period is only one part of the cycle. In adolescents, cycles commonly last 21 to 45 days, and bleeding generally lasts no more than seven days. Cycles can be irregular during the first few years. A 28-day example is not a deadline that every body must meet.

Some people experience cramps or discomfort. Talk to a trusted adult or health professional about very heavy bleeding, severe pain, a gap of more than three months between periods, or any worry. Having a concern checked is more useful than comparing private experiences with classmates.

Much later in life, menstrual periods stop naturally at **menopause**, usually between ages 45 and 55. This is different from the temporary irregularity that may occur when periods first begin. A person’s needs change across life, and reliable information and care remain important.

No scientific reason supports treating a menstruating person as impure or isolating them. People can learn, play and take part in daily life during periods, with rest or support when needed. Privacy, clean facilities and freedom from teasing help everyone participate comfortably.

paragraphs: A learner misses a school activity because there is no private place to change a pad. Someone says that periods themselves prevent participation.
Separate the body process from the problem with facilities. What practical changes could the school make? Explain why support should not require anyone to announce that they are menstruating.
lesson.addition: Distinguish a biological process from barriers to participation.

lesson.text: 6.3  Feelings and Behaviour

Growing up may bring stronger feelings, changing interests, a wish for independence or increased sensitivity to others’ opinions. Some adolescents experience mood changes; others do not notice large changes. There is no single emotional pattern that everyone must experience.

paragraphs: 1. Discuss fictional situations: being left out of a game, excited about a hobby or upset after criticism. Do not name real people.
2. Record possible feelings, responses and constructive alternatives in your notebook. Use Table 6.2; several responses may be reasonable.
3. Consider music, dance, sport, creativity and helping others. Nobody needs to disclose private experiences.

lesson.caption: Table 6.2  Feelings, responses and choices
rows: Pause, talk and try a manageable activity
Clarify what was meant; discuss calmly
lesson.note: These are examples, not predictions about every adolescent. Read across for alternatives; add a different response in your notebook.

lesson.text: Feelings do not dictate actions. Anger need not lead to harm, nor curiosity to risk. Pause, name the feeling and consider another viewpoint. Creative interests can support learning and cooperation.

Support matters when sadness, worry or other feelings persist, interfere with everyday life or feel difficult to manage. Speak to a trusted adult, counsellor or health professional. Asking for help is a useful action, not a personal failure. Respect another person’s privacy when they seek support.
6.4  Caring for Health and Well-being

Food, hygiene, movement, relationships and access to help contribute to well-being. Healthy habits take practice and support. A useful plan fits a person’s needs; it does not depend on looking like someone else.
6.4.1  Meeting Nutritional Needs

A growing body needs a varied diet. Carbohydrates and fats supply energy; proteins support growth and repair. Vitamins and minerals help many body processes. Calcium supports bones, and iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the substance in red blood cells that carries oxygen.

paragraphs: 1. List affordable local foods and seasonal choices in your notebook. Do not compare classmates’ lunches or family spending.
2. Identify nutrients and their functions using a reliable food guide, label or teacher’s guidance. Record your information source.
3. Compare with Table 6.3. Suggest a varied day’s meals and explain why several foods are needed.

lesson.caption: Table 6.3  Foods, nutrients and their roles
rows: Milk, curd, cheese, paneer; calcium-rich ragi millet
Pulses, beans, eggs, fish or other suitable protein foods
Growth and repair; can also supply energy
Rice, roti and other grains; oils and nuts
Spinach, kidney beans, raisins and figs
lesson.note: Examples, not a complete diet prescription. Read across for a connection; compare down for variety. Nutrient amounts depend on food, portion and preparation.

lesson.text: A food name does not tell us everything about a meal. Portion size, variety, preparation and the foods eaten over time matter. Plant foods can supply iron, but the body does not absorb all sources equally. Vitamin-C-rich foods such as guava or lemon can help the absorption of iron from plant foods.

For example, a meal with roti or rice, dal, vegetables and curd combines foods with different contributions. If one ingredient is unavailable, ask which local alternative could serve a similar purpose. Planning variety is more useful than searching for a single “perfect” food or dividing all foods into simply good and bad.
lesson.addition: Apply nutrient variety to an affordable meal and substitutions.

lesson.text: Too little iron or vitamin B12 can contribute to **anaemia**, in which the blood has too few healthy red blood cells or too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen effectively. Anaemia also has other causes. Tiredness alone cannot diagnose it. A health professional can assess a concern and advise suitable care.

Find out how your school or local health centre supports good nutrition. India’s Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation programme and Anaemia Mukt Bharat include measures to reduce anaemia. Ask the teacher or health worker how the local programme works. Take supplements only through appropriate professional or programme guidance.

Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin used X-ray studies to work out the structures of important molecules, including vitamin B12. She received the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and was the third woman to receive that chemistry prize. Her work connects molecular structure with health. We need dietary sources of B12; discuss suitable foods with your teacher.
6.4.2  Personal and Menstrual Hygiene

Bathe regularly, change into clean clothes and wash hands at appropriate times. Gently clean areas where sweat collects, including the armpits and external genital region. Cleanliness supports comfort and health; strong perfumes and harsh products are not substitutes for washing. Everyone deserves private, accessible washing and toilet facilities.

lesson.caption: Clean pads, washing supplies and a covered bin are parts of practical menstrual hygiene support.

columns.title: Disposable pads
items: Use a clean pad and change it regularly, sooner if wet or soiled. Follow product guidance.
Wrap a used pad in paper or its wrapper. Put it in the designated bin; never flush it.

columns.title: Reusable cloth pads
items: Use a clean, dry pad made for this purpose. Change it regularly.
Wash with soap and clean water, dry completely, and store clean and dry. Follow the maker’s care instructions.

lesson.text: Wash hands before and after changing a pad. A school needs clean water, soap, privacy and a safe disposal system as well as access to products. Ask a trusted adult for help obtaining supplies. Nobody should be mocked for carrying a pad or needing to change one.

Some products are described as biodegradable, but this does not mean that they may be littered, flushed or composted at home. Disposal depends on the material and the local waste system. Follow local guidance; environmental claims do not replace safe collection and disposal.
Where Support Can Be Found

items: **Menstrual Hygiene Scheme (MHS):** supports menstrual-hygiene awareness and access to pads for adolescent girls in rural areas.

**Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK):** supports adolescent health, including nutrition, mental health and menstrual health. Trained peer educators can help connect young people with information and services.
**Jan Aushadhi Suvidha:** makes affordable sanitary pads available through Jan Aushadhi Kendras.

**State programmes:** examples include Karnataka’s Shuchi scheme and pad-distribution programmes in Tamil Nadu and Odisha. Ask a local school or health worker about current eligibility and availability.

lesson.text: Programmes and supplies differ between places. A trained health worker or adolescent-friendly health clinic can explain local services. Share information respectfully without publicly identifying who needs help.
6.4.3  Movement and Rest

Regular physical activity supports fitness, stamina and mood. Games, walking, dance, cycling and suitable exercises can all provide movement. Choose safe activities that you enjoy and that suit your abilities. Inclusive games let participants take different roles instead of excluding someone who moves differently.

lesson.caption: Activity can be adapted so that friends with different abilities participate together.

lesson.text: Balance active time with rest and regular sleep. Drink safe water, use appropriate equipment and follow a teacher’s guidance for unfamiliar exercises. Pain or dizziness is a reason to stop and seek help, not a challenge to push through. Being active is about well-being, not achieving a particular body shape.
lesson.addition: Accessible participation and proportionate exercise precautions.

lesson.text: 6.4.4  Friendships and Digital Life

Friendships, cooperation and new interests can become especially important in adolescence. Some people feel attraction to peers. Respectful behaviour includes listening, accepting another person’s boundaries and avoiding pressure. You do not have to copy a group’s actions to deserve friendship.

Online tools can help us learn, create and stay in touch. They also allow messages and pictures to spread beyond the audience first intended. Ask permission before sharing someone’s image or information. A person known only online may not be who they claim to be.

**Cyberbullying** is bullying through digital devices or services. Examples include repeated hurtful messages, spreading rumours and sharing private information to embarrass someone. If this happens, tell a trusted adult. With their help, save relevant evidence, use blocking or reporting tools, and avoid forwarding harmful material.

lesson.caption: A trusted adult can help a learner respond to an online problem without spreading the harmful message.

lesson.text: Being frightened or upset does not make someone responsible for bullying. If one adult does not help, approach another. Friends can refuse to join in and help the person find support.

paragraphs: 1. Design a group poster or pamphlet about responsible social-media behaviour. Use fictional examples, with no personal photos, private messages or identifying details.
2. List helpful actions and actions to avoid in your notebook. Compare with Table 6.4 and explain your suggestions.
3. Check clarity and kindness. With teacher approval, display your work in a designated school space. Ask readers which action they could take.

lesson.caption: Table 6.4  Responsible choices online
rows: Insults, rumours and joining in with bullying
Forwarding a claim just because it is popular
Sharing private photos or details with strangers or online-only contacts
Seek trusted help and report problems
Handling threats alone or spreading hurtful screenshots
lesson.note: Read each row as a pair. Add a practical example in your notebook without naming real people.

paragraphs: A chat shares an embarrassing picture. Would forwarding it “so others know what happened” increase the harm? Explain.
Distinguish keeping evidence privately for a trusted adult from circulating it. Suggest a response that supports the learner and protects privacy.
lesson.addition: Apply the difference between evidence preservation and harmful redistribution.

lesson.text: 6.4.5  Saying No and Seeking Help

Tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedis, alcohol and harmful or illegal drugs can damage health. A friend or an older person may pressure someone to try them. A firm “No, I do not want to” is enough. Move away from an unsafe situation and seek help from a trusted adult; you do not need to win an argument.

Consider a friend who says, “Everyone is trying it.” You could reply, “I am not joining in. Let us do something else.” If the pressure continues, leave with someone you trust. Practise the words with a fictional situation; never bring tobacco, alcohol or drugs into a classroom demonstration.
lesson.addition: Concrete refusal and exit example, with no real substances used.

lesson.text: Some substances can cause **addiction**: a health condition involving strong urges and difficulty controlling use despite harm. The risk varies, but “just once” does not guarantee safety or the ability to stop. Addiction is not inevitable after one use, and a person who needs help should not be blamed or mocked.

lesson.caption: An explanatory comparison: tobacco smoke harms airways and lung tissue. This is not a picture of how every affected lung looks.

lesson.text: The effects depend on the substance and exposure. Tobacco smoke can damage the lungs and make breathing difficult. Alcohol and other drugs can affect judgement, memory and physical or mental health. Avoiding harmful substances protects health; prescribed medicines should be used only as directed.

A person finding it hard to stop needs support, counselling and sometimes medical treatment. A trusted adult can help contact a health professional. Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, led by India’s Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, promotes prevention and community awareness. The National De-addiction Helpline is **14446**.
6.5  Why Do These Changes Occur?

Many changes at puberty are coordinated by **hormones**, chemical messengers made in the body. They travel in the blood and act on particular cells or organs. Signals involving the brain and hormone-producing glands help regulate growth and reproductive development.

lesson.caption: Hormonal signals act alongside nutrition, health and inherited differences.

lesson.text: Hormones influence feelings, but sleep, relationships, experiences and surroundings also matter. Dismissing a worry as “just hormones” can prevent someone from receiving support.

Adolescence includes common processes and individual differences. Reliable information, respectful relationships and healthy routines help. Questions are welcome; discuss private concerns with trusted people who can offer appropriate guidance.

glossary.purpose: Reference definitions for terms taught in the chapter
entries: Adolescence
The stage between childhood and adulthood, usually defined as ages 10–19.
Puberty
Physical changes through which the body develops reproductive capability.
Secondary sexual characteristics
Features developing at puberty that are not the reproductive organs themselves.
Larynx
The voice box, containing the vocal folds that vibrate to produce sound.
Acne
A skin condition involving blocked follicles and inflammation, often producing pimples.
Menstruation
The shedding of part of the uterine lining, with blood, through the vagina.
Menopause
The natural end of menstrual periods later in adult life.
Hormones
Chemical messengers that help regulate body processes.
Anaemia
A condition in which blood has too few healthy red blood cells or too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen effectively.
Addiction
Difficulty controlling substance use despite harm, often with strong urges.

summary: Adolescence, usually ages 10–19, connects childhood and adulthood. Physical, emotional and social development do not follow an identical timetable for everyone.
Height, body shape, voice, skin and hair may change. Variation is expected, and people deserve privacy and respect.
Secondary sexual characteristics develop during puberty but are not the reproductive organs. Puberty brings reproductive capability; this is not the same as readiness for adult responsibilities.
Menstruation is one phase of the menstrual cycle. Teen cycles commonly last 21–45 days, with variation especially early on. Menopause usually occurs much later, between ages 45 and 55.
Feelings can influence behaviour, but we can pause, consider choices and ask for support. No single emotional pattern describes every adolescent.
A varied diet supplies energy, protein, vitamins and minerals. Iron and vitamin B12 help healthy blood formation; concerns about deficiencies need appropriate assessment.
Hygiene, menstrual supplies, private facilities, safe disposal, physical activity and rest support health and participation.
Respect boundaries and privacy in person and online. Do not share harmful messages or private images; seek trusted help for bullying.
Avoid tobacco, alcohol and harmful drugs. Addiction needs supportive care, not blame. Trusted adults and health services can help.
Hormones help coordinate growth and puberty. Reliable information and guidance help young people understand changes and make informed choices.

assessment.purpose: All ten source questions retained with safety and evidence qualifications

questions.text: Ramesh, aged 11, notices pimples on his face. (a) Explain how changes during puberty may contribute to acne. (b) Suggest gentle skin-care habits and explain when he should seek professional advice.

Compare the two food arrangements below. Which offers a better starting point for varied everyday meals during adolescence, and why? Discuss nutrients, variety and portions; do not judge a person’s diet from one meal.
questions.caption: (i) Burger, fries, pizza and doughnuts.  (ii) A meal with grains, dal, vegetables, salad and curd.

questions.text: Unscramble the words in your notebook. (a) The shedding of the uterine lining with blood is nstmnoiaretu. (b) Growth of the iceov xob can change the voice. (c) Physical development towards reproductive capability is urtypeb. (d) We should avoid lahoclo and harmful srugd. Explain one answer in your own words.
Shalu says, “Adolescence brings only physical changes, such as growing taller or developing body hair.” Is this complete? Rewrite her description to include other kinds of development.

What questions would you ask to examine these claims? (a) Adolescents do not need to pay attention to changes in behaviour. (b) A person who tries a harmful substance once can stop whenever they want. Explain what reliable information would help assess each claim.

Some adolescents notice changing moods. What other changes in interests, feelings or behaviour may occur? Give examples of constructive responses, and explain why these examples should not become labels for all adolescents.

Mohini notices used pads scattered near a toilet bin. What menstrual-hygiene habits and school facilities would help? Discuss clean products, handwashing, privacy and disposal. Explain how to report the problem without blaming or identifying anyone.

Mary, aged 11, and Manoj, aged 12, both notice a change at the front of the neck. After examination, a doctor identifies iodine-related thyroid enlargement in Mary and ordinary larynx growth in Manoj. Why is the advice different? Use the two structures taught in the chapter. Why would looking at a photograph be insufficient to decide whether treatment is needed?

Group these changes: voice change, breast development, moustache growth, other facial hair, pimples, pubic hair and armpit hair. Use “common in boys and girls”, “typically more pronounced in boys” and “typically seen in girls”. Explain where a change can belong in more than one description, and why “only” may be misleading.

Make a poster offering practical tips for well-being during adolescence. Include food, hygiene, activity, respectful relationships and access to help. Use inclusive language and avoid judging appearance.

projects.title: Find Out About Local Support
projects.text: With your teacher, identify a person or organisation supporting young people’s mental health. Prepare at least five questions about their work, available help, privacy, access and ways schools can support learners. Let the teacher arrange any interview and obtain permission before recording. Do not collect anyone’s diagnosis or personal history. Summarise the service information in your notebook.

projects.title: A Role Play About Childhood and Choice
projects.text: Create a fictional role play about how child marriage can harm health, education, safety and opportunities, particularly for girls. Show a young person receiving support from trusted adults. Explain why puberty is not readiness for marriage or parenthood. Avoid using real classmates’ experiences or making anyone disclose private information. Discuss what a supportive community could do.

projects.title: Plan an Inclusive Yoga Session
projects.text: International Yoga Day is observed on 21 June. With a trained teacher, plan a small session of suitable asanas and gentle movement. Provide comfortable alternatives, including seated participation, and make participation voluntary. Never force a stretch or hold the breath. Stop if there is pain or dizziness and tell the teacher. Reflect on how clear guidance and inclusion helped the session.
